title: Optimize screen font definition and storage
body:
## Goal
Optimize the way the screen font is defined to replace the current huge array with a more efficient approach.

## Context
The current screen font implementation uses a huge array to define character bitmaps, which is inefficient in terms of memory usage and maintainability. This approach makes the kernel binary larger and harder to modify or extend with different fonts.

## Definition of Done
- Analyze the current font array implementation and identify optimization opportunities
- Research and implement a more efficient font storage format (compressed bitmaps, vector fonts, or external font files)
- Reduce memory footprint while maintaining or improving rendering performance
- Add support for multiple font sizes or styles if feasible
- Ensure backward compatibility with existing font rendering functionality
- Update font loading and character rendering code to work with the new format
- Document the new font system architecture and how to add or modify fonts
- Verify that all text rendering continues to work correctly after optimization

title: Refactor code structure to make it more organized
body:
## Goal
Refactor the codebase structure to improve organization, maintainability, and development workflow.

## Context
The current code structure could benefit from better organization to make it easier for developers to navigate, understand, and contribute to the project. A well-organized codebase improves maintainability, reduces technical debt, and makes it easier to locate and modify specific functionality.

## Definition of Done
- Analyze current code structure and identify areas for improvement
- Create a logical directory structure that groups related functionality
- Separate concerns properly (kernel core, drivers, memory management, etc.)
- Establish consistent naming conventions across the codebase
- Refactor header file organization and includes
- Update build system (Makefile) to reflect new structure
- Ensure all existing functionality continues to work after refactoring
- Document the new code organization and contribution guidelines
- Update any documentation that references old file paths or structure

title: Implement proper hardware probing and driver connection
body:
## Goal
Detect hardware properly and connect to the respective drivers for further development.

## Context
The current hardware probing implementation doesn't do much beyond basic initialization. The system needs a proper hardware detection mechanism that can identify available hardware components and automatically connect them to their appropriate drivers.

## Definition of Done
- Implement comprehensive hardware detection during system initialization
- Create a driver registry system that maps hardware IDs to driver implementations
- Automatically probe and enumerate available hardware (PCI devices, USB controllers, network cards, etc.)
- Establish proper driver loading and connection mechanisms
- Add logging/debugging output to show detected hardware and loaded drivers
- Provide a foundation for future driver development and hardware support expansion
- Document the hardware probing process and driver architecture

title: Create cross-compiler toolchain for userland
body:
## Goal
Set up a cross-compiler toolchain that targets meniOS userland ABI.

## Context
Part of the Road to Doom infrastructure. We need a complete toolchain (binutils + GCC/Clang) that can compile user programs for meniOS, including Doom.

## Definition of Done
- Configure and build cross-binutils for meniOS target
- Build cross-GCC or Clang targeting meniOS userland ABI
- Create linker scripts for user program layout
- Implement basic C runtime startup code (crt0)
- Create minimal libc subset with essential functions
- Set up build system for compiling userland programs
- Document toolchain installation and usage
- Test toolchain by compiling simple test programs

## Dependencies
- Syscall ABI definition
- Process memory layout specification

title: Implement filesystem support and VFS layer
body:
## Goal
Create filesystem support with VFS layer and basic file operations for userland.

## Context
Part of the Road to Doom infrastructure. User processes need to access files, especially Doom needs to load WAD assets from disk.

## Definition of Done
- Implement block device driver (AHCI/ATA or RAM-backed disk)
- Create filesystem implementation (FAT32 or simple custom FS)
- Build VFS (Virtual File System) abstraction layer
- Implement syscalls: open, read, write, lseek, close, stat
- Add directory traversal support (opendir, readdir, closedir)
- Support file metadata and permissions
- Handle file system mounting and unmounting
- Test with loading large files (for Doom WAD assets)

## Dependencies
- Syscall interface
- Block device driver infrastructure

title: Implement userspace graphics/framebuffer interface
body:
## Goal
Create userspace-accessible graphics interface for rendering applications like Doom.

## Context
Part of the Road to Doom infrastructure. Doom needs to render graphics at 320×200 or 640×480 resolution with 8-bit or 32-bit color depth.

## Definition of Done
- Expose framebuffer to userspace through syscalls or memory mapping
- Support multiple video modes (320×200, 640×480) with different bit depths
- Implement double-buffering to avoid screen tearing
- Add page-flip or buffer swap syscalls
- Support 8-bit paletted mode and palette control
- Implement basic blitting operations for performance
- Add optional software scaling for resolution conversion
- Ensure thread-safe access to graphics resources

## Dependencies
- Syscall interface
- Virtual memory management
- Existing framebuffer improvements

title: Implement userspace input subsystem
body:
## Goal
Create userspace input interface for keyboard and mouse input.

## Context
Part of the Road to Doom infrastructure. Doom needs keyboard input for controls and mouse input for looking/turning.

## Definition of Done
- Create userspace keyboard interface using PS/2 driver
- Implement event queue or character device for keyboard input
- Add mouse driver with relative motion and button support
- Create input event system for userspace applications
- Support both raw scancodes and cooked keyboard events
- Implement input buffering and non-blocking reads
- Add proper input device management and multiplexing
- Test input responsiveness for gaming applications

## Dependencies
- PS/2 keyboard driver improvements
- Syscall interface
- Mouse driver implementation

title: Implement audio subsystem for userspace
body:
## Goal
Create audio output system that userspace applications like Doom can use.

## Context
Part of the Road to Doom infrastructure. Doom requires audio output for sound effects and music playback.

## Definition of Done
- Implement PCM audio output driver (AC97, HDA, or PC speaker fallback)
- Create audio mixing and streaming syscalls
- Support 8-bit and 16-bit audio sample formats
- Implement audio buffer management and DMA transfers
- Add timer-driven audio callbacks or asynchronous queue system
- Support multiple audio streams/channels for sound effects + music
- Handle audio sample rate conversion if needed
- Test with simple audio playback before Doom integration

## Dependencies
- Syscall interface
- Hardware audio driver
- Timer/interrupt management

title: Implement preemptive userland scheduler
body:
## Goal
Create a preemptive scheduler that can manage userland processes with proper time slicing.

## Context
Part of the Road to Doom infrastructure. User processes need to be scheduled fairly and Doom needs consistent timing for smooth gameplay.

## Definition of Done
- Implement preemptive scheduling for user processes
- Add time slicing with configurable quantum lengths
- Support process priorities and scheduling policies
- Implement per-process accounting and statistics
- Add sleep/yield primitives for user threads
- Handle scheduler interaction with kernel threads
- Support process state management (running, sleeping, waiting)
- Ensure smooth scheduling for real-time applications like games

## Dependencies
- Process management infrastructure
- Timer/interrupt handling
- Context switching mechanism

title: Improve kmalloc implementation
body:
## Goal
Enhance the kmalloc implementation to be more robust, efficient, and feature-complete.

## Context
The current kmalloc implementation is basic and could benefit from improvements in performance, reliability, and functionality. As the kernel grows and especially as we move toward userland support, memory allocation becomes increasingly critical.

## Definition of Done
- **Performance improvements**: Optimize allocation/deallocation algorithms for better speed and reduced fragmentation
- **Better debugging**: Add allocation tracking, leak detection, and corruption detection
- **Size alignment**: Ensure proper memory alignment for different data types and architectures
- **Error handling**: Improve error reporting and graceful handling of allocation failures
- **Memory pools**: Consider implementing size-based memory pools for common allocation sizes
- **Statistics**: Add memory usage statistics and monitoring capabilities
- **Integration**: Better integration with virtual memory management system
- **Bounds checking**: Add optional bounds checking to detect buffer overflows
- **Thread safety**: Ensure kmalloc is thread-safe for multi-threaded kernel operations

## Potential Improvements
- Implement buddy allocator or slab allocator for better performance
- Add kmalloc_aligned() for specific alignment requirements
- Implement kcalloc() and krealloc() for completeness
- Add memory poisoning for debugging (fill freed memory with pattern)
- Consider adding memory zones (DMA, normal, high memory)
- Add allocation size classes to reduce fragmentation

title: Improve kmutex implementation
body:
## Goal
Enhance the existing kmutex implementation to be more robust, efficient, and feature-complete for kernel synchronization.

## Context
The current kmutex implementation provides basic mutual exclusion but could benefit from improvements in performance, debugging capabilities, and additional features needed for a robust kernel synchronization primitive.

## Definition of Done
- **Performance improvements**: Optimize lock/unlock operations for minimal overhead
- **Debugging support**: Add lock tracking, deadlock detection, and ownership validation
- **Priority handling**: Implement priority inheritance to prevent priority inversion
- **Timeout support**: Add kmutex_lock_timeout() for non-blocking operations with timeouts
- **Recursive locks**: Support for recursive mutex acquisition by the same thread
- **Error handling**: Improve error reporting and validation of mutex operations
- **Statistics**: Add lock contention statistics and performance monitoring
- **Documentation**: Comprehensive API documentation with usage examples

## Potential Improvements
- Add kmutex_trylock() for non-blocking lock attempts
- Implement fair scheduling to prevent lock starvation
- Add mutex debugging modes (leak detection, double-lock detection)
- Support for different mutex types (normal, recursive, errorcheck)
- Integration with kernel debugging and profiling tools
- Lock ordering validation to detect potential deadlocks

title: Implement semaphore synchronization primitive
body:
## Goal
Implement counting semaphores for kernel synchronization and resource management.

## Context
Semaphores are essential synchronization primitives that allow controlling access to a finite number of resources. They're particularly useful for producer-consumer scenarios, resource pools, and implementing other synchronization constructs.

## Definition of Done
- **Core functionality**: Implement ksem_init(), ksem_wait(), ksem_post(), ksem_destroy()
- **Counting semaphore**: Support for initial count and maximum count values
- **Timeout support**: Add ksem_wait_timeout() for non-blocking waits with timeout
- **Try operations**: Implement ksem_trywait() for non-blocking attempts
- **Error handling**: Proper error codes and validation for all operations
- **Thread safety**: Ensure all operations are atomic and thread-safe
- **Performance**: Optimize for minimal overhead in common use cases
- **Integration**: Work seamlessly with kernel scheduler and thread management

## Use Cases
- Resource pool management (memory pools, connection pools)
- Producer-consumer synchronization
- Rate limiting and flow control
- Barrier implementation
- Building higher-level synchronization primitives

title: Implement read-write locks (rwlock)
body:
## Goal
Implement read-write locks to allow concurrent read access while maintaining exclusive write access.

## Context
Read-write locks are crucial for scenarios where data is frequently read but infrequently modified. They allow multiple readers to access shared data concurrently while ensuring exclusive access for writers.

## Definition of Done
- **Core functionality**: Implement rwlock_init(), rwlock_read_lock(), rwlock_write_lock(), rwlock_unlock()
- **Reader priority**: Allow multiple concurrent readers
- **Writer exclusivity**: Ensure writers have exclusive access
- **Fairness**: Prevent writer starvation when many readers are present
- **Try operations**: Implement rwlock_try_read_lock() and rwlock_try_write_lock()
- **Timeout support**: Add timeout versions for non-blocking operations
- **Upgrade/downgrade**: Support for upgrading read locks to write locks (optional)
- **Debug support**: Lock tracking and validation in debug builds

## API Design
- rwlock_t data structure
- rwlock_init() - Initialize read-write lock
- rwlock_read_lock() - Acquire read lock (shared)
- rwlock_write_lock() - Acquire write lock (exclusive)
- rwlock_unlock() - Release lock (read or write)
- rwlock_try_read_lock() - Non-blocking read lock attempt
- rwlock_try_write_lock() - Non-blocking write lock attempt

## Use Cases
- Shared data structures with frequent reads, infrequent writes
- Cache implementations
- Configuration data protection
- File system metadata
- Network routing tables
- Database-like operations in kernel

title: Implement condition variables
body:
## Goal
Implement condition variables for thread coordination and event-driven synchronization.

## Context
Condition variables are essential for implementing wait/notify patterns where threads need to wait for specific conditions to become true. They work in conjunction with mutexes to provide efficient blocking and signaling mechanisms.

## Definition of Done
- **Core functionality**: Implement kcond_init(), kcond_wait(), kcond_signal(), kcond_broadcast()
- **Mutex integration**: Work seamlessly with kmutex for atomic condition checking
- **Spurious wakeup handling**: Proper semantics for condition variable waits
- **Timeout support**: Add kcond_wait_timeout() for bounded waiting
- **Signal semantics**: Both single-thread signal and broadcast to all waiters
- **Error handling**: Proper error codes and validation
- **Performance**: Efficient implementation with minimal overhead

## API Design
- kcond_t data structure
- kcond_init() - Initialize condition variable
- kcond_wait() - Wait for condition (releases mutex, reacquires on wakeup)
- kcond_wait_timeout() - Wait with timeout
- kcond_signal() - Wake up one waiting thread
- kcond_broadcast() - Wake up all waiting threads
- kcond_destroy() - Clean up condition variable

## Use Cases
- Producer-consumer patterns
- Thread pool work queue management
- Event notification systems
- Implementing barriers and rendezvous
- Resource availability notifications
- Complex synchronization patterns requiring state-based waiting

title: Enable SMP (Symmetric Multiprocessing) support
body:
## Goal
Add support for multiple CPU cores to enable true multiprocessing capabilities in meniOS.

## Context
Currently meniOS runs on a single CPU core. Adding SMP support will enable the kernel to utilize multiple cores, improving performance and enabling true parallel processing. This is essential for modern systems and will be important for running complex applications like Doom with better performance.

## Definition of Done
- **CPU Detection**: Detect and enumerate available CPU cores using ACPI tables
- **AP Initialization**: Boot and initialize Application Processors (non-boot CPUs)
- **Per-CPU Data**: Implement per-CPU data structures and variables
- **SMP-Safe Synchronization**: Ensure all kernel data structures are SMP-safe
- **SMP Scheduler**: Extend scheduler to distribute tasks across multiple CPUs
- **Load Balancing**: Basic load balancing between CPU cores
- **CPU Affinity**: Support for binding processes/threads to specific CPUs
- **SMP-Safe Memory Management**: Make memory allocators and VM system SMP-safe

## Key Components to Implement
- **ACPI Parsing**: Parse MADT (Multiple APIC Description Table) to find CPU cores
- **APIC Configuration**: Set up Local APIC and I/O APIC for inter-processor communication
- **AP Boot Protocol**: Implement CPU startup sequence for secondary cores
- **Spinlocks**: Implement proper spinlocks for SMP synchronization (depends on issue #38)
- **Per-CPU Variables**: Implement __percpu data and accessor functions
- **SMP-Safe Primitives**: Update all shared data structures with proper locking
- **CPU Hotplug**: Basic support for CPU online/offline operations (optional)

## Technical Challenges
- **Bootstrap Process**: Complex CPU initialization sequence
- **Memory Barriers**: Proper memory ordering between CPUs
- **Race Conditions**: Identify and fix all potential race conditions in kernel
- **Cache Coherency**: Handle CPU cache synchronization issues
- **Interrupt Distribution**: Distribute interrupts across multiple CPUs
- **Atomic Operations**: Hardware-specific atomic instructions (see issue #41)

## Dependencies
- Issue #38: Spinlock implementation (critical for SMP)
- Issue #41: Atomic operations and memory barriers
- Improved synchronization primitives for SMP-safe operations

## Testing Strategy
- Start with 2-CPU system, expand to 4+ cores
- Stress testing with concurrent operations
- Verify proper load distribution across cores
- Test interrupt handling on multiple CPUs
- Validate memory consistency across cores

## Performance Benefits
- Parallel execution of kernel threads
- Better responsiveness under load
- Improved performance for multi-threaded applications
- Foundation for userland multi-threading support
- Better utilization of modern hardware

title: Evolve mosh shell to be the default userland shell for meniOS
body:
## Goal
Evolve the basic shell implementation in `app/mosh` (meniOS shell) to become the default userland shell for meniOS with essential bash-like functionality.

## Context
Currently, there's a very basic shell implementation in `app/mosh` that serves as a starting point. As meniOS progresses toward full userland support, we need a functional shell that users can interact with to launch programs, navigate the filesystem, and perform basic system operations.

## Definition of Done
- **Command parsing**: Parse basic command lines with arguments
- **Built-in commands**: Implement essential built-ins (cd, ls, pwd, exit, help)
- **Program execution**: Launch userland programs via exec syscalls
- **File operations**: Basic file manipulation (cat, cp, mv, rm) when filesystem is available
- **Environment**: Basic environment variable support
- **History**: Simple command history functionality
- **Tab completion**: Basic filename/command completion (nice-to-have)
- **Error handling**: Proper error messages and graceful failure handling
- **Prompt customization**: Configurable prompt showing current directory

## Implementation Details
- Build upon existing code in `app/mosh/`
- Keep implementation simple and lightweight for educational OS
- Focus on core functionality rather than advanced features
- Integrate with meniOS syscall interface
- Design for single-user, single-session usage initially

## Built-in Commands to Implement
- `cd [directory]` - Change current directory
- `ls [directory]` - List directory contents
- `pwd` - Print working directory
- `cat <file>` - Display file contents
- `echo <text>` - Print text to console
- `help` - Show available commands
- `exit` - Exit shell
- `clear` - Clear screen

## Dependencies
- Syscall interface (write, read, open, close, etc.)
- Filesystem support and VFS layer
- ELF loader for launching programs
- Process management for userland programs
- Basic userland C library functions

## Integration Points
- Launch as default shell after kernel boot
- Integrate with userland process lifecycle
- Work with meniOS filesystem when implemented
- Provide platform for testing other userland applications

## Future Enhancements
- Job control (background processes)
- Pipes and redirection
- Shell scripting capabilities
- More advanced built-ins
- Configuration files

## Files to Work With
- `app/mosh/` - Existing shell implementation
- Integration with userland build system
- Documentation for shell usage

## Testing Strategy
- Test basic command parsing and execution
- Verify built-in commands work correctly
- Test error handling for invalid commands
- Validate integration with filesystem operations
- Ensure proper cleanup on exit

This shell will serve as the primary user interface for meniOS and provide a platform for testing other userland applications, including eventually launching Doom! 🎮

title: Implement per-CPU data infrastructure
body:
## Goal
Create per-CPU data infrastructure to support SMP by ensuring each CPU has distinct stacks, runqueues, stats, and other CPU-local data.

## Context
Essential SMP foundation. Once multiple CPUs are running, each needs isolated data structures to avoid race conditions and improve performance. This includes CPU-local stacks, runqueues, statistics, and temporary storage.

## Definition of Done
- **Per-CPU allocator**: Implement percpu_alloc() and percpu_free() functions
- **Per-CPU macros**: Create macros for declaring and accessing per-CPU variables
- **CPU-local stacks**: Separate kernel stacks for each CPU
- **CPU-local runqueues**: Individual scheduler runqueues per CPU
- **CPU-local statistics**: Per-CPU counters and performance metrics
- **CPU ID management**: Reliable way to get current CPU ID
- **Memory layout**: Efficient memory layout for per-CPU data sections

title: Implement APIC/MADT CPU enumeration
body:
## Goal
Parse ACPI MADT (Multiple APIC Description Table) to enumerate CPU cores and prepare for Application Processor (AP) startup.

## Context
Essential SMP foundation. Before bringing up additional CPUs, we need to discover how many cores are available, their LAPIC IDs, and other CPU-specific information from the ACPI tables.

## Definition of Done
- **ACPI MADT parsing**: Parse MADT table to find CPU entries
- **CPU enumeration**: Build list of available CPUs with their LAPIC IDs
- **CPU information storage**: Store CPU topology and capabilities
- **BSP identification**: Identify Bootstrap Processor vs Application Processors
- **CPU state tracking**: Track CPU states (offline, online, booting)
- **LAPIC base address**: Extract Local APIC base address from MADT
- **Error handling**: Handle malformed or missing ACPI tables gracefully

title: Implement AP startup and BSP → AP bring-up
body:
## Goal
Initialize Application Processors (APs): set up startup trampoline, per-CPU GDT/TSS, switch to long mode, and hand off to C code.

## Context
Core SMP implementation. After CPU enumeration, we need to wake up the Application Processors and get them running kernel code alongside the Bootstrap Processor.

## Definition of Done
- **Startup trampoline**: Real-mode trampoline code to bootstrap APs
- **AP initialization sequence**: Complete AP startup from real mode to long mode
- **Per-CPU GDT/TSS**: Separate GDT and TSS for each CPU
- **Per-CPU stacks**: Dedicated kernel stacks for each AP
- **SIPI protocol**: Send Startup IPI to wake up APs
- **Synchronization**: Coordinate AP startup with BSP
- **C handoff**: Transfer AP control to C kernel code
- **Error handling**: Handle AP startup failures gracefully

title: Extend scheduler for SMP with per-CPU runqueues
body:
## Goal
Extend the scheduler to support SMP with per-CPU runqueues, load balancing, and inter-processor interrupt (IPI) based reschedules.

## Context
SMP scheduler foundation. Once multiple CPUs are running, the scheduler needs to distribute work across cores, balance load, and handle cross-CPU scheduling decisions.

## Definition of Done
- **Per-CPU runqueues**: Separate runqueue for each CPU core
- **Load balancing**: Migrate tasks between CPUs to balance load
- **IPI reschedules**: Send IPIs to trigger reschedules on other CPUs
- **CPU affinity**: Support for binding tasks to specific CPUs
- **Idle CPU handling**: Proper idle loop and work stealing
- **Scheduler statistics**: Per-CPU scheduling statistics and metrics
- **SMP-safe operations**: All scheduler operations protected with appropriate locks

title: Implement interrupt distribution and IPIs
body:
## Goal
Implement interrupt distribution and Inter-Processor Interrupts (IPIs) to properly distribute device IRQs and enable CPU-to-CPU communication.

## Context
SMP interrupt handling. Multiple CPUs need coordinated interrupt handling, with device interrupts distributed across cores and IPIs enabling CPU-to-CPU communication for scheduling and other kernel operations.

## Definition of Done
- **Device interrupt distribution**: Distribute device IRQs across multiple CPUs
- **IPI framework**: Send and receive inter-processor interrupts
- **LAPIC programming**: Configure Local APIC for IPI generation/reception
- **IOAPIC programming**: Configure I/O APIC for interrupt routing
- **IPI types**: Support for reschedule, function call, and TLB flush IPIs
- **Interrupt affinity**: Control which CPU handles specific interrupts
- **Performance optimization**: Minimize interrupt latency and overhead

title: Audit kernel structures for SMP safety
body:
## Goal
Audit critical kernel subsystems to ensure they are SMP-safe with proper spinlock protection or per-CPU isolation.

## Context
SMP safety audit. Before enabling multiple CPUs, all shared kernel data structures must be protected against race conditions through appropriate synchronization mechanisms.

## Definition of Done
- **Subsystem audit**: Review all critical kernel subsystems for SMP safety
- **Lock identification**: Identify what locks are needed for each shared structure
- **Per-CPU conversion**: Convert appropriate structures to per-CPU where beneficial
- **Lock implementation**: Add spinlocks/mutexes to protect shared data
- **Documentation**: Document locking rules and conventions
- **Testing**: Verify SMP safety under stress testing

title: Add SMP testing and diagnostics
body:
## Goal
Add comprehensive testing and diagnostic capabilities for SMP functionality including smoke tests, CPU verification, and cross-CPU locking validation.

## Context
SMP validation and debugging. Once SMP is implemented, we need robust testing to ensure it works correctly and diagnostic tools to debug issues.

## Definition of Done
- **SMP smoke tests**: Basic tests to verify multiple CPUs are operational
- **CPU enumeration tests**: Verify all CPUs are detected and brought online
- **Cross-CPU communication tests**: Test IPI delivery and handling
- **Lock contention tests**: Stress test spinlocks and synchronization
- **Performance benchmarks**: Measure SMP performance gains
- **Diagnostic tools**: Tools to monitor CPU states and activity
- **Failure diagnosis**: Tools to debug SMP bring-up failures
